title: Imports and Reuse of the Parent Cramer Result
content: Three imports power this file: `Mathlib.Data.Nat.Factorial.Basic` for `Nat.factorial_pos` and the factorial API; `Mathlib.Tactic` for the omnibus tactic suite (`linarith`, `nlinarith`, `ring`, `omega`, `positivity`, `interval_cases`, `native_decide`); and `Proofs.CramersRuleOQ02` — the parent gallery proof that establishes Gaussian-vs-Cramer asymptotics. Importing the parent lets us *re-export* its key definitions and theorems (`gaussMuls`, `cramersRuleMuls`, `gauss_beats_cramer`, `cramer_asymptotically_worse`, `cramersRuleMuls_eq`, `factorial_gt_sq`) and reuse them without duplication. This is the cleanest pattern for extending a research result: build on the existing namespace rather than copying the lemmas.
mathContext: Inheritance: $\text{gaussMuls}(n) := n^3, \quad \text{cramersRuleMuls}(n) := (n+1) \cdot n \cdot n!, \quad \text{factorial\_gt\_sq}: n^2 < n! \text{ for } n \geq 4.$

title: Namespace Setup: CramersComplexityLUQR
content: We open the parent namespace `CramersComplexity` so unqualified references to `gaussMuls`, `cramersRuleMuls`, etc., resolve directly. The new namespace `CramersComplexityLUQR` keeps the LU/QR additions logically separate while still benefiting from the parent's content. `open Nat` brings `factorial_pos`, `Nat.factorial_gt_sq` (re-exported through the parent), and arithmetic helpers into scope for compact tactic invocations.
mathContext: Namespace hierarchy: `CramersComplexity` ⊃ `CramersComplexityLUQR`. The child extends the parent's complexity-model vocabulary with LU and QR functions.

title: LU and QR Complexity Functions
content: Two new complexity models are defined. `luMuls n := n³` captures LU decomposition's roughly $n^3/3$ multiplications, conservatively rounded up to $n^3$ — the same asymptotic bound used for Gaussian elimination in the parent. `qrMuls n := 2·n³` models QR factorization via Householder reflections, which costs roughly $4n^3/3$ flops; we round up to $2n^3$ to keep the constants small integers and avoid rational arithmetic. The conservative rounding is intentional: any inequality proved against this upper bound is also true of the actual algorithm. These are the *only two definitions* in the file — every other declaration is a theorem.
mathContext: $\text{luMuls}(n) := n^3, \quad \text{qrMuls}(n) := 2 \cdot n^3.$ Real-world flops counts: LU $\approx n^3/3$, QR-Householder $\approx 4n^3/3$. The model rounds *up* to keep integer arithmetic, which weakens the comparison in our favor (anything we prove for $2n^3$ is true for $4n^3/3 \leq 2n^3$).

title: LU = Gaussian by `rfl`
content: `luMuls n = gaussMuls n` holds by *definitional equality* (`rfl`): both unfold to `n^3`. This is the conceptual content of the design choice — modeling LU at the same granularity as Gaussian. The `rfl` proof is a feature, not a coincidence: it means every theorem about `gaussMuls` automatically applies to `luMuls` without further work, and the LU theorems below reduce to the parent's Gaussian results by simple rewriting.
mathContext: $\text{luMuls}(n) = \text{gaussMuls}(n)$ — definitional, since both are $n^3$ in our model.

title: Gaussian ≤ QR ≤ 2·Gaussian
content: Three short ordering lemmas pin down the within-O(n³) hierarchy. `gaussMuls_le_qrMuls n` is $n^3 \leq 2n^3$ — discharged by `linarith` once `simp only` unfolds the definitions. `qrMuls_le_two_gaussMuls n` is $2n^3 \leq 2n^3$ — discharged by `le_refl _` (literal equality). Combined into `lu_qr_constant_factor n` which packages the symmetric statement that LU and QR are within a factor of 2. This *is* the formal statement that LU and QR are in the same complexity class.
mathContext: $n^3 = \text{luMuls}(n) \leq \text{qrMuls}(n) = 2n^3 \leq 2 \cdot \text{luMuls}(n) = 2n^3.$ The constant factor between LU and QR is at most 2, so they are in the same big-O class.

title: LU Beats Cramer (Direct Reduction)
content: Because `luMuls = gaussMuls`, the LU-vs-Cramer theorems reduce immediately to the parent's `gauss_beats_cramer`. `lu_beats_cramer` for $n \geq 4$ is just a direct application; `lu_beats_cramer_all` extends to $n \geq 1$ by case-splitting on $n < 4$ vs $n \geq 4$ and discharging the small cases ($n=1,2,3$) by `interval_cases <;> native_decide` — Lean evaluates both sides numerically. This pattern (use `native_decide` for the residual base cases that fall below the algebraic threshold of the asymptotic argument) recurs throughout the file.
mathContext: $\forall n \geq 1, \, \text{luMuls}(n) = n^3 < (n+1) \cdot n \cdot n! = \text{cramersRuleMuls}(n).$ Small cases verified: $n=1: 1 < 2; \, n=2: 8 < 12; \, n=3: 27 < 72.$

title: Key QR Lemma: 2n³ < n²·n! for n ≥ 4
content:
The technical heart of the QR side. We need $2n^3 < n^2 \cdot n!$ — strictly stronger than the Gaussian inequality $n^3 < n^2 \cdot n!$. The proof factors into three concrete steps composed by `linarith`:

1. **$2n^3 < n \cdot n^3$**: since $2 < n$ (from $n \geq 4$) and $n^3 > 0$, multiply on the right by `Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_right`.
2. **$n \cdot n^3 = n^2 \cdot n^2$**: pure algebra, discharged by `ring`.
3. **$n^2 \cdot n^2 < n^2 \cdot n!$**: invoke the parent's `factorial_gt_sq hn` ($n^2 < n!$ for $n \geq 4$), then multiply on the left by `Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_pos_left` with $n^2 > 0$ from `positivity`.

The conceptual move: split off a factor of $n$ from $2n^3$ to get $n^2 \cdot n^2$, then leverage that $n^2$ already satisfies the factorial bound. The factor-of-2 penalty for QR is absorbed by the $n \cdot n^3$ vs $2n^3$ comparison, which turns into a factor of $n/2$ — and $n/2 \geq 2$ exactly when $n \geq 4$, matching the threshold for `factorial_gt_sq`.
mathContext: $2n^3 < n \cdot n^3 = n^2 \cdot n^2 < n^2 \cdot n! \quad (n \geq 4).$ Each strict inequality contributes; `linarith` chains them.

title: QR Beats Cramer for n ≥ 4 (and n ≥ 3 by Computation)
content:
`qr_beats_cramer` for $n \geq 4$: rewrite via `qrMuls` and `cramersRuleMuls_eq`, apply the key lemma to get $2n^3 < n^2 \cdot n!$, then bridge to $(n+1) \cdot n \cdot n!$ via $n^2 = n \cdot n \leq (n+1) \cdot n$ (a tiny `nlinarith` step). The chained inequality $2n^3 < n^2 \cdot n! \leq (n+1) \cdot n \cdot n!$ closes by `linarith`.

`qr_beats_cramer_from_3` extends down to $n \geq 3$: the algebraic argument breaks at $n = 3$ (we'd need $2 < 3$ in step 1, which is true, but `factorial_gt_sq` requires $n \geq 4$). Instead we case-split, handle $n = 3$ by `subst this; native_decide` ($2 \cdot 27 = 54 < 72 = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 6$), and let the algebraic case handle $n \geq 4$. The threshold $n = 3$ is the crossover point: at $n = 2$ QR is *worse* than Cramer ($16 > 12$), so we cannot extend below.
mathContext: Crossover: $n=1: \text{qr}=2, \text{cr}=2$ (tie); $n=2: \text{qr}=16 > 12 = \text{cr}$ (QR worse!); $n=3: \text{qr}=54 < 72 = \text{cr}$ (QR wins). The strict inequality starts at $n = 3$.

title: Asymptotic K-Factor Superiority of QR
content:
The crown of the file: for *any* constant $K$, there exists a threshold $N$ beyond which $K \cdot \text{qrMuls}(n) < \text{cramersRuleMuls}(n)$. The witness $N := \max(4, 2K)$ has two parts:
- $N \geq 4$ ensures `factorial_gt_sq` applies.
- $N \geq 2K$ ensures $K \cdot 2 \leq n$ — which after multiplying on the right by $n^3$ gives $K \cdot (2n^3) \leq n \cdot n^3$.

The rest reuses the algebraic chain from the key lemma: $n \cdot n^3 = n^2 \cdot n^2 < n^2 \cdot n! \leq (n+1) \cdot n \cdot n!$. Three named steps `step1`/`step2`/`step3` make the dependencies explicit; `linarith` composes them. This is the formal statement that QR is *unboundedly* better than Cramer for large enough $n$ — no constant factor of QR can keep up with the factorial growth of Cramer.
mathContext: $\forall K \in \mathbb{N}, \, \exists N = \max(4, 2K), \, \forall n \geq N: \quad K \cdot 2n^3 \leq n \cdot n^3 = n^2 \cdot n^2 < n^2 \cdot n! \leq (n+1) \cdot n \cdot n!.$

title: Three-Way Comparison Theorem
content: Packages the full hierarchy `luMuls n = gaussMuls n ≤ qrMuls n < cramersRuleMuls n` (for $n \geq 4$) into a single conjunction. The proof is just `⟨luMuls_eq_gaussMuls n, gaussMuls_le_qrMuls n, qr_beats_cramer hn⟩` — three previously-proved facts assembled. This is the API a downstream caller wants: one theorem giving the complete relative ordering of the three cubic algorithms against the factorial baseline.

title: All Cubic Algorithms Beat Cramer Asymptotically
content: The strongest statement of the file: a single theorem says that *every* member of the cubic family — Gaussian, LU, QR — is asymptotically K-times better than Cramer for any $K$. Since `luMuls = gaussMuls`, the LU witness is identical to the Gaussian one (`cramer_asymptotically_worse K`); QR uses the new `qr_asymptotically_better K`. The conjunction-of-existentials structure is exactly what readers want to cite: 'pick any $K$, any of the cubic algorithms eventually beats Cramer by $K$.' This is the formal counterpart of the textbook claim 'cubic algorithms vastly outperform Cramer.'
mathContext: $\forall K: \, \exists N_g, N_l, N_q: \, \forall n \geq N_*: K \cdot n^3 < (n+1) \cdot n \cdot n!.$ Three witnesses, but in our model $N_g = N_l$ (since LU and Gaussian coincide) and $N_q$ is shifted by the $2n^3$ factor.

title: Master Summary: lu_qr_vs_cramer_summary
content: A 5-clause master conjunction summarising the entire file: (1) the LU/Gauss model identity, (2) the QR/Gauss factor-of-2 relationship, (3) LU beats Cramer for $n \geq 4$, (4) QR beats Cramer for $n \geq 4$, (5) the asymptotic K-factor superiority of QR. Each component reuses theorems proved earlier — no new mathematics, just packaging. This is the canonical entry point a paper or downstream proof would cite: one theorem, all the facts.
mathContext: Conjunction of: $\text{luMuls} = \text{gaussMuls}; \, \text{qrMuls} = 2 \cdot \text{gaussMuls}; \, n \geq 4 \implies \text{luMuls}(n) < \text{cr}(n); \, n \geq 4 \implies \text{qrMuls}(n) < \text{cr}(n); \, \forall K \, \exists N: K \cdot \text{qrMuls}(n) < \text{cr}(n).$
